strengths: Addresses an important and timely overclaimed capability in the literature with rigorous empirical evaluation
Elegant decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation that clarifies failure modes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets with systematic testing of multiple resolutions and frequency combinations
Effective use of spectral analysis and aliasing concepts to understand and visualize failure modes
Practical solution with computational analysis showing multi-resolution training can be cost-effective using primarily low-resolution data
Thorough evaluation of competing approaches (physics-informed constraints, band-limited learning) rather than just claiming superiority
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the proposed solution—multi-resolution training is straightforward data augmentation that practitioners would naturally attempt; the positive contribution is incremental
Primary focus on FNO despite claiming to evaluate MLOs broadly; CNO and CROP receive limited evaluation, leaving generalizability across architectures unclear
Insufficient analysis of why previous papers claimed zero-shot capability; no investigation of whether their experimental setups or resolution ratios differed
Incomplete causal analysis: limited exploration of why physics-informed constraints fail beyond 'optimization difficulty,' and band-limited learning evaluation is somewhat cursory
Core OOD argument is somewhat circular—defining training distribution by resolution then noting different resolutions are OOD; continuous operator perspectives might handle this differently
Evaluation limited to three PDEs; would benefit from more diverse PDE types, different problem characteristics, and non-PDE scientific problems
Reliance on L2 loss alone; additional metrics (relative error, spectral norms, maximum error) would strengthen claims
Missing theoretical analysis of when/why multi-resolution training should work beyond empirical observation; lacks connection to active learning and curriculum learning literatures
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or reporting of random seeds; hyperparameters optimized at specific resolutions then transferred to others potentially biases results
Limited practical discussion: how expensive is multi-resolution data generation in practice? When is zero-shot actually needed versus feasible?

strengths: Addresses an important and timely claim in the MLO literature by rigorously testing zero-shot super-resolution capabilities
Systematic experimental decomposition into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation components
Appropriate use of Fourier analysis and energy spectra to diagnose aliasing failures with clear visualization
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard datasets with extensive supplementary materials
Practical finding that models can achieve multi-resolution performance with mostly low-resolution training data
Evaluation of multiple proposed solutions (physics-informed constraints, band-limited learning) goes beyond single-method critique
weaknesses: Core finding lacks novelty: applies well-established generalization principles (models fail on out-of-distribution data) to a specific domain rather than providing new insights
Proposed solution is trivial and obvious: multi-resolution training is a straightforward application of known principles with no sophisticated data selection strategy
Narrow architectural scope: experiments focus heavily on FNO; generalization to other MLO architectures (DeepONet, G-Transformer, etc.) is assumed but not demonstrated
Inadequate statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis; appears to be single runs

Incomplete treatment of alternatives: physics constraints tested on one implementation only; band-limited learning critique is somewhat circular; no engagement with broader ML literature (transfer learning, meta-learning, active learning)
Strawmanning original claims: FNO's claim was discretization-invariance for fixed PDE families, not arbitrary frequency content changes; inflammatory framing ('False Promise') oversimplifies

Experimental design concerns: synthetic data via low-pass filtering may not reflect real use cases; hyperparameter tuning on single resolution then applied universally; multi-resolution-specific tuning unexplored
Limited mechanistic understanding: documents failures but provides minimal insight into why models assign energy to unseen frequencies or what learned representations capture
Trivial multi-resolution training analysis: no ablations on sampling strategies, minimum high-resolution data requirements, or which resolutions matter most
Missing important related work and baselines from transfer learning, domain adaptation, curriculum learning, and meta-learning literature

strengths: Clear identification and framing of an important gap between claims in prior work and actual MLO capabilities
Rigorous decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation components
Excellent diagnostic methodology using energy spectra and normalized residuals to visualize aliasing artifacts
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with systematic variation of training/test resolutions and independent hyperparameter tuning
Thorough evaluation of alternative solutions (physics-informed constraints, band-limited learning) with clear explanations of limitations
Practical multi-resolution training solution with valuable efficiency insights (70-90% low-res, 10-30% high-res suffices)
Exceptional thoroughness with extensive appendices, ablations, and reproducibility details
Well-written with clear presentation, good signal processing contextualization, and compelling visualizations
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope: analysis focuses heavily on FNO; broader claims about 'MLOs' lack sufficient supporting evidence from diverse architectures
Core insight is relatively straightforward from generalization theory perspective (changing resolution ≈ OOD inference)
Multi-resolution training solution is obvious given problem formulation; lacks technical novelty or innovation
Incomplete analysis of band-limited approaches: Section 4.2 shows they work reasonably well for their intended purpose; dismissal is somewhat unfair
Limited theoretical analysis of *why* neural operators fail at frequency extrapolation beyond standard OOD intuition
Physics-informed constraints evaluation could be deeper: results showing data loss outperforms data+physics loss warrant investigation of root causes beyond optimization difficulty
Missing analysis of learned representations: what do FNOs learn at different resolutions and why does this prevent frequency extrapolation?
Limited dataset diversity: three smooth PDE benchmarks only; no real-world applications or complex domains tested
Practical limitation not emphasized: solution still requires some high-resolution data, partially defeating 'zero-shot' motivation
Cost-benefit analysis incomplete: comparison of total cost (low-res + high-res data) versus training on high-res alone would be valuable

strengths: Rigorous and systematic experimental evaluation with clear decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple datasets, architectures, and platforms with excellent reproducibility (hyperparameter details, code promised, cross-architecture testing)
Effective use of spectral analysis to diagnose aliasing and OOD generalization failures; more informative than scalar metrics alone
Evaluates previously proposed solutions (physics constraints, band-limited learning) and explains why they fail, not just critiquing FNO
Practical multi-resolution training solution with substantial efficiency gains (96% dataset reduction, 86% training time reduction) while maintaining performance
Clear presentation with effective figures and systematic approach that could serve as a template for evaluating operator generalization
weaknesses: Limited novelty: multi-resolution training is well-known from prior work (Li et al. 2024a, George et al. 2024, etc.); contribution is primarily empirical validation of efficiency gains
Core finding that models fail to generalize to OOD data is expected from ML theory; while framing in operator/signal processing context is useful, the fundamental insight is not surprising
Narrow architectural scope: only FNO systematically evaluated; DeepONet relegated to appendix with minimal exploration; unclear if findings generalize to other mesh-invariant operators
Somewhat artificial experimental setup: testing extreme resolution gaps (single resolution training) is not the practical use case; practitioners would naturally start with multi-resolution training
Limited theoretical insight: purely empirical work without theoretical analysis of when/why MLOs fail or information-theoretic limits; Section K's anti-aliasing analysis is limited
Narrow physical scope: only three standard PDE benchmarks, no real-world data, all smooth systems; unclear generalization to turbulent flows or systems with shocks

Incomplete multi-resolution training exploration: no principled guidance for selecting resolution ratios beyond empirical Pareto front; no exploration of curriculum learning or progressive training strategies
Presentation length (54 pages) with redundancy across datasets makes core contributions difficult to extract; paper could be more concise

strengths: Thorough experimental validation across multiple datasets, architectures, and resolutions with comprehensive appendices including multi-seed analysis and cross-platform benchmarking
Clear pedagogical decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation
Systematic evaluation of proposed solutions (physics-informed constraints, band-limited learning) across multiple methods
Practical analysis of data-cost tradeoffs in multi-resolution training with Pareto frontier visualization
Technically sound experimental work with appropriate spectral analysis and multiple evaluation metrics
weaknesses: Limited novelty: multi-resolution training is already widely used (cited in 8+ prior works); the core finding that models don't generalize to out-of-distribution data is unsurprising and well-established in ML

Unclear what prior claims are being refuted: the paper attributes zero-shot super-resolution claims to FNO and others, but these prior works make more nuanced claims than presented; appears somewhat like a strawman argument

Artificial experimental setup: artificial frequency truncation via low-pass filtering doesn't reflect realistic scenarios; resolution interpolation and information extrapolation experiments are contrived compared to actual use cases

Minimal mechanistic insight: explanations reduce to 'out-of-distribution' without deeper analysis of what enables or could enable generalization; aliasing discussion is classical signal processing, not novel

Limited architectural scope: only Fourier-based methods tested (FNO, CNO, CROP); overreaching title/abstract claims about 'Machine-Learned Operators' broadly when conclusions apply narrowly to specific architectures

Questionable baseline evaluations: physics-informed constraints evaluation may be limited by hyperparameter choices; band-limited learning methods designed for fixed-resolution are unfairly compared to OOD scenarios
Code not available at review time, only promised upon acceptance
Missing theoretical framework and no exploration of whether zero-shot could work under different problem formulations or with novel architectural designs

strengths: Rigorously challenges important claim about MLO capabilities with comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures, datasets, and hardware platforms
Clever decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and information extrapolation, providing clear diagnosis of failure modes
Excellent grounding in signal processing theory (Nyquist-Shannon sampling, aliasing) that makes the analysis principled and insightful
Exemplary experimental practices: multiple random seeds, ablations on design choices (max modes, activations, downsampling methods), and cross-platform validation
Clear practical guidance showing multi-resolution training with mostly low-resolution + some high-resolution data provides good performance-cost tradeoff
Effective visualization of aliasing artifacts through spectral energy analysis convincingly demonstrates both problem and solution
Strong reproducibility commitment with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and code release promise
Systematic evaluation of alternative approaches (physics-informed constraints, band-limited learning) showing why they fail to address core issue
weaknesses: Limited novelty of proposed solution: multi-resolution training is straightforward and previously explored; contribution is primarily diagnostic rather than methodological
Theoretical analysis could be deeper: out-of-distribution explanation is intuitive but lacks formal generalization theory; unclear why MLOs specifically suffer compared to other approaches
Scope limitations: FNO dominates main paper while other architectures (DeepONet, CNO) relegated to appendices; claims about 'machine-learned operators' generally may be overstated
Limited guidance on optimal multi-resolution training: how to select resolutions and data ratios remains unresolved beyond empirical Pareto frontier
Generalization concerns: only standard PDE benchmarks evaluated; unclear if findings extend to other domains or problem classes
Statistical rigor: multiple seeds only for Darcy dataset; more extensive statistical testing and confidence intervals would strengthen claims
Missing exploration of conditions for zero-shot success: paper characterizes failures but doesn't identify problem classes where zero-shot might work
Incomplete analysis of when/why certain design choices matter (e.g., specific filter limit values, downsampling strategies)
